summary: A country on the eastern Mediterranean coast whose capital, Damascus, and Aleppo are among the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world; it fell into civil war in 2011, and the Assad regime collapsed at the end of 2024.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Arab Muslim armies conquered Syria in 634–640, and after the defeat of the Byzantines at the Battle of the Yarmouk in 636, the Umayyad dynasty made Damascus its capital in 661 and built the Umayyad Mosque in the early 8th century. Over the following centuries the inhabitants gradually converted to Islam, and Sunni rule under the Ottoman Empire from 1516 to 1918 further consolidated its position. Sunni Muslims are the main faith of the Arabs, Kurds and Turkmen and are found throughout the country, especially concentrated in cities such as Damascus, Aleppo and Homs.

ranking.name: Alawism
ranking.description: Alawism originated in a 9th-century branch of Shia Islam and, because its doctrines differ from the mainstream, was long persecuted by Sunni rulers, and its followers withdrew to the coastal mountains of the west around Latakia and Tartus. During the French Mandate (1920–1946) large numbers of Alawites were recruited into the army, and in 1970 Hafez al-Assad, of Alawite background, seized power in a coup; the Assad family then ruled Syria for half a century until the regime collapsed in December 2024. They are still concentrated in the western coastal region.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Syria is one of the oldest cradles of Christianity: the apostle Paul was converted on the road to Damascus, and Antioch was also one of the earliest church centers, so there are ancient churches such as the Greek Orthodox, Syriac Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches. After the Armenian genocide of 1915 large numbers of survivors fled to Aleppo, enlarging the Christian community. Before the outbreak of the civil war in 2011 Christians made up about one tenth of the population, and war and emigration have greatly reduced the share.

ranking.name: Druze
ranking.description: The Druze faith split off in the 11th century from the Ismaili branch under the Fatimid dynasty of Egypt; its doctrines are secret and it does not accept converts, and to escape persecution its followers settled in mountain areas. The Druze of Syria are concentrated in the southern province of Suwayda, the "Druze Mountain," where in 1925 Sultan al-Atrash led the Great Syrian Revolt against the French, giving the Druze an important place in national history.

ranking.name: Other Shia (Twelver, Ismaili)
ranking.description: The center of the Ismailis is Salamiyah near Hama, which in the 9th century was a base for secret Ismaili preaching, and today its followers take the Aga Khan as their spiritual leader. The Twelvers are scattered in a few villages around Damascus and Aleppo, and the Sayyidah Zaynab shrine in Damascus is an important Shia pilgrimage site. Both are minorities in a country with a Sunni majority.

religion.background: Syria is one of the places where Christianity first spread; after the Arab conquest of the 7th century Islam gradually became the majority, and Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad dynasty. From the Middle Ages, minority sects such as the Alawites, Druze and Ismailis formed settlements in the mountains, and the Ottoman Empire ruled for four hundred years under a Sunni-dominated order. From 1970 the Assad family, of Alawite background, held power, and the civil war that broke out in 2011 deepened religious and ethnic antagonism and drove large numbers of Christians and other minorities to leave. After the collapse of the Assad regime in December 2024, the situation of religious minorities has become an important issue in national reconstruction.

ranking.name: Arabic (Levantine dialect)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest of Syria in the 7th century, Arabic gradually replaced the formerly common Aramaic and Greek, and Damascus, as capital of the Umayyad dynasty, was a center of Arab culture. The local spoken language belongs to the Levantine Arabic dialects, close to the dialects of Lebanon, Jordan and Palestine, while schools and the media use Modern Standard Arabic. The Ba'ath government long pursued Arab nationalism, so Arabic is the mother tongue of the great majority of citizens.

ranking.name: Kurdish
ranking.description: The Kurds are distributed mainly in the north and northeast around Hasakah, Afrin and Kobani and speak the Kurmanji dialect, and many of them are descendants of Kurds who crossed the border to settle from the 1920s to escape Turkish repression. A special census by the government in 1962 left more than a hundred thousand Kurds stateless, and during the Ba'ath period teaching Kurdish in schools was also banned. During the civil war in 2012 the Kurds established an autonomous administration and began running schools and publishing in Kurdish.

ranking.name: Armenian
ranking.description: Most Armenian speakers are descendants of survivors of the 1915 Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire, who after fleeing to cities such as Aleppo built schools, churches and associations that kept the language alive. Aleppo was therefore once one of the most important centers of the Armenian community in the Middle East, but after the civil war of 2011 large numbers of Armenians moved to Armenia, Lebanon and Western countries, and their numbers have fallen markedly.

language.history: In ancient Syria Akkadian and Aramaic were in common use; Aramaic was the everyday language of the time of Jesus, and in villages such as Maaloula north of Damascus some people still speak Western Aramaic today. After the Arab conquest of the 7th century Arabic gradually became the mainstream, and Damascus was a center of Arab culture under the Umayyad dynasty. During the French Mandate French was an elite language, and after independence the Ba'ath Party pursued Arabization policies. Kurdish in the north and Armenian in Aleppo reflect the migration and ethnic history of the 20th century.

ranking.name: Kibbeh
ranking.description: A shell kneaded from cracked wheat (bulgur) and ground meat, filled with fragrant minced meat, onion and pine nuts, shaped like an olive and deep-fried; there are also baking-tray and raw versions.
ranking.history: Bulgur is a traditional wheat product of the Levant going back thousands of years, and kibbeh, in which it is pounded to a paste together with meat, is regarded as the national dish of Syria and Lebanon. The large northern city of Aleppo, at a crossroads of the Silk Road, is famous for its spices and cooking and is said to make dozens of different kinds of kibbeh, such as versions cooked with sour cherries or yogurt. In the days before meat grinders, women had to pound the meat in a stone mortar for a long time, so kibbeh was a labor-intensive dish made for festivals and entertaining guests.

ranking.name: Shawarma
ranking.description: Marinated chicken or lamb is stacked in layers on a vertical rotating spit and slowly roasted, then shaved into thin slices and put into flatbread with garlic sauce, pickles and fries.
ranking.history: The technique of vertical rotating grilled meat took shape in the 19th century around Bursa in the Ottoman Empire and then spread throughout the empire, and the name "shawarma" comes from the Turkish "çevirme" (turning). In the Levant it was given garlic sauce and pickles and became the most common fast food on the streets of Damascus and Aleppo. Since the 20th century Syrian and Lebanese immigrants have taken shawarma to Europe, the Americas and the Gulf states, and the wave of refugees after the 2011 civil war has led to Syrian shawarma shops opening throughout Germany and elsewhere.

ranking.name: Fattoush salad
ranking.description: Fresh vegetables such as tomato, cucumber, lettuce, radish and mint are tossed with pieces of toasted or fried Arabic bread and seasoned with sumac, lemon juice and olive oil.
ranking.history: Fattoush originated in the rural Levant, and its name comes from the Arabic "fatt" (to crumble); it was originally a frugal practice of farmers who tore up stale bread left overnight and added it to a salad. The sour, purple-red sumac is a spice used locally since ancient times and gives the salad its unique flavor. Today it is a regular on meze platters and one of the most common salads at the iftar meal that breaks the fast in Ramadan.

ranking.name: Muhammara
ranking.description: Roasted red peppers pounded with walnuts, breadcrumbs, pomegranate molasses and cumin into a thick red spread, sweet, spicy and slightly sour, often served with Arabic bread.
ranking.history: This dip is generally believed to have originated in Aleppo, and its name comes from the Arabic word for "red." Chili peppers are native to the Americas and reached the Middle East in the 16th century through the Ottoman trade network; around Aleppo the famous "Aleppo pepper" later developed and became the soul of muhammara. Pomegranate molasses and walnuts are local products from ancient times, reflecting the culinary tradition of Aleppo, a trade-route city, in blending old and new ingredients.

ranking.name: Baba ghanoush (roasted eggplant dip)
ranking.description: Eggplants are roasted directly over charcoal until the skin is charred and the inside is soft, then peeled and mashed and mixed with tomato, onion, pomegranate molasses or tahini, with a rich smoky aroma.
ranking.history: The eggplant is native to India and was introduced to the Middle East and widely grown there in the 8th–10th centuries during the Arab Empire through the "Arab Agricultural Revolution," becoming one of the most important vegetables of Levantine cuisine. The name literally means "spoiled father," and various folk stories about the origin of the name circulate, but there is no settled account. In Syria the version with tahini is often called "mutabbal," while the one with vegetables such as tomato is called baba ghanoush; both are common home appetizers.
